title: India Just Shipped Its First Semiconductor Chips Abroad. Modi Will Inaugurate the Plant Tomorrow.
excerpt: CG Semi's Sanand facility sent its first commercial chips to Malaysia, and a ₹1.25 lakh crore second wave of investment is already approved.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India exported its first semiconductor chips to Malaysia, marking a historic milestone.
  • CG Semi's Sanand facility aims for an annual capacity of 5 billion chips.
  • The government approved ₹1.25 lakh crore for the India Semiconductor Mission 2.0.
  • India is focusing on mature-node chips, avoiding cutting-edge sub-7nm fabrication.
  • The semiconductor push is creating job opportunities and attracting diaspora talent.

On June 19, a cargo plane left Gujarat's Sanand industrial zone carrying something India had never exported before: commercially manufactured semiconductor chips. The shipment — assembled and tested at CG Semi's pilot facility for Japanese chipmaker Renesas — landed in Kuala Lumpur, marking a milestone that decades of Indian prime ministers had pursued and failed to deliver. Two weeks later, the story is accelerating. Prime Minister Narendra Modi will inaugurate CG Semi's full ₹7,500-crore Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) facility at Sanand on Saturday, formally starting commercial production at one of India's first semiconductor packaging and testing plants under the India Semiconductor Mission. ## From Pilot Line to Production Floor CG Semi, a subsidiary of the Chennai-based Murugappa Group's CG Power, operates the Sanand plant in partnership with Japan's Renesas Electronics and Thailand's Stars Microelectronics. The pilot line — inaugurated by Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw in August 2025 — has been qualifying products for months. The first commercial shipment validated that the facility can produce chips that meet international standards. The numbers are ambitious. Once fully ramped up, the Sanand plant will have an annual production capacity of up to 5 billion semiconductor chips, serving customers across automotive, industrial, telecommunications, 5G and IoT sectors. The pilot G1 facility is currently running at about 500,000 units per day; the larger G2 facility is expected to be operational by the end of 2026. CG Semi provides end-to-end semiconductor assembly and testing services — wafer sorting, assembly, testing, package design, failure analysis, test programme development, and logistics support. Renesas, which holds about a 7 per cent stake, is the anchor customer and technology partner. ## Twelve Factories, Four Going Live The Sanand inauguration is not an isolated event. It arrives in a month when India's semiconductor mission is hitting several milestones at once. Vaishnaw told the CII Annual Business Summit in May that India now has two semiconductor plants in commercial production, a third starting in July — the CG Semi facility — and a fourth expected to come online by November or December. Work on 12 semiconductor factories is currently in progress across multiple states. The other major projects include Tata Electronics' ₹91,526-crore semiconductor fabrication plant at Dholera, Gujarat, being built in partnership with Taiwan's Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation (PSMC). This will be India's first 300mm wafer fab, targeting mature-node chips at 28nm to 110nm — the workhorses that power everything from automotive microcontrollers to 5G modems. Tata has also partnered with Dutch equipment giant ASML to deploy lithography tools at the Dholera fab, a deal announced during Modi's visit to the Netherlands. Micron Technology's $2.75-billion assembly, test, marking and packaging (ATMP) facility, also at Sanand, has completed Phase 1 and is ramping toward high-volume commercial production of DRAM and NAND memory products. Kaynes Technology is building another OSAT plant at Sanand. ## The ₹1.25 Lakh Crore Second Wave The Centre has approved a budget of around ₹1.25 lakh crore for the India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 — substantially higher than the ₹76,000 crore earmarked for the first phase. The allocation signals that New Delhi sees semiconductors as a strategic priority on par with defence and space. In May alone, the Cabinet approved two more projects under ISM: the country's first commercial Mini/Micro-LED display facility based on gallium nitride technology (by Crystal Matrix Limited in Dholera) and a new semiconductor packaging facility — together worth ₹3,936 crore. Four additional projects were approved earlier, including facilities by SiCSem, Continental Device India, 3D Glass Solutions, and ASIP Technologies, bringing total approved projects to 10 with cumulative investments of about ₹1.6 lakh crore across six states.

The Design Linked Incentive scheme, running in parallel, is nurturing a pipeline of fabless chip design startups that could eventually feed India's own packaging and test ecosystem. ## What India Can — and Cannot — Make India is not pursuing cutting-edge sub-7nm fabrication — those require extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines that are controlled by export restrictions and available from a single supplier. Instead, the strategy is anchored around 28nm and above, which accounts for the vast majority of global semiconductor demand outside smartphones and high-end computing. This is a deliberate bet. Automotive electronics, EV powertrains, power management, industrial IoT, telecom infrastructure — these sectors consume enormous volumes of mature-node chips, and their demand is growing faster than leading-edge. India's pitch is that it can be a reliable, geopolitically neutral source for these workhorses at a time when the world is desperate to diversify away from concentration in Taiwan, South Korea and China. NITI Aayog estimates India will need $135–180 billion in investment over the next decade to build a globally competitive semiconductor ecosystem. The Centre cannot shoulder this alone, but sustained public funding is designed to de-risk private investment. ## The Diaspora Dimension For NRIs in the semiconductor industry — and there are thousands, from design engineers in the Bay Area to process engineers in Dresden and Hsinchu — India's chip push is creating a reverse-brain-drain opportunity that didn't exist five years ago. Several diaspora-founded chip design companies have set up India operations to plug into the growing domestic ecosystem, and the talent pipeline is expanding rapidly. Vaishnaw noted that AI job opportunities in India are growing 15–20 per cent annually, and that Google has agreed to manufacture AI servers in the country. The semiconductor buildout is a foundational layer for all of it. The first shipment from Sanand was a box of chips on a cargo plane. What it represented was a country that had spent 60 years trying to enter the semiconductor supply chain — and finally did.
